context.requirement_text:
Second half of ISS-0431/GH#835's fix for its own stated PRIMARY
surface, atop REQ-216's core module. Mirrors REQ-186/REQ-187's and
REQ-214/REQ-215's own "core module first, wiring requirement(s)
second, disjoint files" split precedent in this file.

TWO ADMISSION GATES, NOT ONE, because tenant identity is not known
until partway through `Letflow.Plugs.ApiPipeline`'s existing chain --
read in full (lib/letflow/plugs/api_pipeline.ex): `Plug.Parsers` runs
first, then `assign_trace_id`, then `Letflow.Plugs.AuthPipeline`
(which itself resolves tenant identity via a DB read -- token
verification, tenant-by-realm/slug resolution, JIT provisioning --
i.e. AuthPipeline's OWN work already consumes a DB connection BEFORE
any tenant identity exists to gate on), then
`Letflow.Plugs.TenantStatus`, then `match`/`dispatch`. Given that
ordering, a single per-tenant-only gate cannot run early enough to
cover AuthPipeline's own connection use. Resolved as follows, stated
as an accepted, disclosed limitation rather than silently glossed
over (matching this project's own honesty convention for a limitation
that cannot be fully closed within one requirement's scope, e.g.
decision 0014's own disclosed WASM native-crash gap):

1. GLOBAL gate, mounted FIRST in the chain -- before `Plug.Parsers`,
so a request rejected for lack of capacity is rejected before any
body-parsing work is spent on it. Calls
`Letflow.Admission.try_acquire(:global)`. Covers AuthPipeline's own
connection use (the gap named above) because it runs before
AuthPipeline and gates ALL downstream DB-connection-holding work,
auth included.
2. PER-TENANT gate, mounted immediately AFTER `Letflow.Plugs.AuthPipeline`
(tenant identity now resolved into `conn.assigns.auth_context.tenant_id`)
and BEFORE `Letflow.Plugs.TenantStatus`/`match`/`dispatch`. Calls
`Letflow.Admission.try_acquire({:tenant, schema_name})`, resolving
`schema_name` the same way `Letflow.Plugs.TenantStatus` and
`Letflow.Scheduler.Poller` already do (tenant-id -> schema-name
resolution already exists in this codebase; reuse it, do not
re-derive). Covers TenantStatus's own DB lookup and every sub-router's
dispatch work -- the dominant share of connection-holding time per
REQ-056/ISS-0431's own round-trip profiling.
DISCLOSED LIMITATION: AuthPipeline's own DB work (steps 1-4 of its
moduledoc) is covered by the global gate only, not a per-tenant one,
because tenant identity does not exist yet at that point in the
chain. This is accepted, not silently omitted -- state it in this
plug's own moduledoc.
3. Both gates: on `{:error, :capacity}`, respond immediately (halt the
plug chain, no further plugs run) via
`Letflow.Api.Response.service_unavailable/2` (REQ-066, ALREADY
EXISTING -- do not add a new response helper), with the
`Retry-After` header set explicitly on the conn first (matching
`Response.rate_limited/2`'s own documented "caller sets Retry-After"
convention) to a fixed, configured seconds value (config, default 1)
-- NOT a computed estimate, since this admission mechanism has no
queueing/backoff-timing model to estimate from (a fixed short value
matching `Letflow.Plugs.TenantStatus`'s own existing `@retry_after_seconds
"30"` precedent's SHAPE, though the specific number here is
independently justified: admission rejection is a near-instant
decision with no wait queue behind it, unlike TenantStatus's
migration-in-progress case, so a MUCH shorter retry-after is
appropriate -- state this reasoning in the plug's moduledoc rather
than copying TenantStatus's 30-second value uncritically).
4. On success at BOTH gates: the plug stores both `admission_ref()`s
in `conn.assigns` and registers a `Plug.Conn.register_before_send/2`
(or equivalent, matching how this codebase already threads
request-scoped cleanup -- state which mechanism is chosen and why) or
calls `Letflow.Admission.release/1` for both refs when the response is
sent, so an admitted request's slot is freed exactly once, on every
response path including a request that raises inside a downstream
plug or router (verified in the acceptance criteria below).
NOT IN THIS REQUIREMENT: no change to REQ-216's core semaphore logic;
no change to `Letflow.Plugs.RateLimit` (still deferred, unmounted,
unrelated mechanism); no Poller wiring (REQ-218); no tier-weighted
per-tenant caps (REQ-216's own recorded open question).

task.description: SECURITY-REVIEWER hard gate on REQ-217 (HTTP admission-control wiring into ApiPipeline), plus an explicit judgment call requested by ORCH on ELIXIR-DEV's own flagged finding: a single HTTP request consumes the GLOBAL admission budget TWICE (once at the global gate, once again as the global half of the per-tenant gate's composing acquisition).

result.summary:
SCOPE TEST: applies. This diff wires a plug into the HTTP entry path (lib/letflow/plugs/api_pipeline.ex) that gates access ahead of every route, and it derives a tenant schema name from resolved identity — enough to run the full INV-1..INV-9 pass rather than a blanket out-of-scope.

INV-1 (tenant isolation): NOT-APPLICABLE in the literal 'Ecto schema/migration/query' sense — this diff adds no Ecto schema, no migration, no query against a business table. The one tenant-derivation step present (Letflow.Plugs.Admission's pool: :tenant branch) reuses conn.assigns.auth_context.tenant_id -> TenantProvisioning.schema_name_for_tenant/1, the SAME derivation AuthPipeline already trusts elsewhere in the same request — never re-derived, never caller-suppliable, and used only to key an in-memory counter (Letflow.Admission holds no Repo call, per its own moduledoc). No cross-tenant data exposure surface exists in this module at all. Confirmed by reading lib/letflow/plugs/admission.ex in full.
INV-2/INV-3/INV-5: NOT-APPLICABLE (S4/S5 not started; this diff shapes no tenant-entity response field and adds no lookup-by-ID endpoint).
INV-4 (secrets): APPLIES (config-resolution is touched: :letflow, :admission, :retry_after_seconds). PASS — grep for hardcoded secret-shaped literals and System.get_env usage across the two changed lib files found nothing; the only config key introduced is a plain integer retry-after value, never security-sensitive.
INV-6 (meta): this handoff itself satisfies it.
INV-7 (no SQL interpolation): APPLIES. `grep -n "Repo.query" lib/letflow/plugs/admission.ex lib/letflow/plugs/api_pipeline.ex` — zero hits. PASS.
INV-8 (no unhandled crashes on realistic failure paths): APPLIES. One heuristic hit: `{:ok, schema_name} = TenantProvisioning.schema_name_for_tenant(tenant_id)` in admission.ex, deliberately left to crash on the believed-unreachable branch (mirrors Letflow.Plugs.TenantStatus's own established fail-closed precedent for a comparably 'should not occur' case, per that plug's own moduledoc and per CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR's step-01d determination that this exact choice is acceptable). Verified real, non-vacuous mutation-testing coverage of both crash branches (missing :auth_context -> KeyError; malformed tenant_id -> MatchError) by reading test/letflow/plugs/admission_test.exs directly — both are exercised by dedicated tests, and ELIXIR-DEV's mutation testing (disabling Mechanism A / Mechanism B independently) each broke exactly the 2 tests designed to catch it, confirmed plausible by reading those specific tests (Mechanism A: 'register_before_send/2 releases on normal completion' + AC3; Mechanism B: 'drains and releases every ref' + AC4). A crash here terminates only the current request (and, under Bandit HTTP/1.1 keep-alive process reuse — confirmed by reading deps/bandit/lib/bandit/http1/handler.ex's maybe_keepalive/2, which reuses one process across a connection's sequential requests — at most the same client's own in-flight work on that connection), never another tenant's. PASS.
INV-9 (SSRF): NOT-APPLICABLE — no outbound HTTP request of any kind in this diff.

AUTH-BYPASS CHECK: read lib/letflow/plugs/admission.ex's call/2 in full. On {:ok, ref} it only assigns two keys and registers a before_send callback, returning the conn otherwise byte-identical (no route dispatch, no halt, no header/body mutation) — a pass-through. On {:error, :capacity} it sets retry-after, calls the pre-existing Response.service_unavailable/2, and halts — no route reachable afterward. The global gate mounted before Plug.Parsers therefore cannot skip or shortcut AuthPipeline; it can only let the full chain proceed unchanged or halt it outright. Confirmed no auth-bypass risk.

RESPONSE-LEAK CHECK: service_unavailable/2 reuses the existing, already-reviewed Error.service_unavailable/1 RFC 9457 shape (REQ-066) — same four fields, no new field. Retry-After is a small fixed integer (config, default 1s), never a computed value that could leak internal timing/capacity numbers. Tenant schema name is never interpolated into the rejection detail string in either branch (@global_rejection_detail / @tenant_rejection_detail are static literals) — confirmed both by reading the source and by test/letflow/plugs/admission_test.exs's own explicit 'no schema name leaked in detail' assertion (refute String.contains?(decoded["detail"], schema)). PASS.

PROCESS-DICTIONARY CROSS-REQUEST LEAK CHECK: read deps/bandit/lib/bandit/http1/handler.ex — Bandit's HTTP/1.1 handler DOES reuse one process across a keep-alive connection's sequential requests (maybe_keepalive/2), so the pdict is NOT strictly per-request; it is per-connection, shared sequentially across that connection's own requests. This means the isolation guarantee is 'no leak across connections/clients', not 'no leak across requests within one keep-alive connection'. Verified this is safe regardless: every normal completion path clears the pdict key via Mechanism A's register_before_send callback (which fires because Plug's own contract requires every conn to be sent, or NotSentError/an exception results), and every pre-dispatch-raise path clears it via Mechanism B's handle_errors/2 (Plug.ErrorHandler's own generated call/2 catches unconditionally). There is no structurally-reachable path that leaves a conn neither sent nor raised, so no stale pdict entry can persist into a next request on a reused connection process. Additionally, even in a hypothetical residual-entry scenario, the pdict holds only opaque admission_ref() counters (no tenant data, no secrets) — a leak here manifests at worst as a capacity-accounting anomaly (an extra release/no-op, per release/1's documented idempotency), never a cross-tenant data disclosure. PASS, with the process-reuse fact now recorded here rather than assumed.

INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION (all commands run by SECURITY-REVIEWER, foreground, real output):
1. `mix compile --warnings-as-errors --force` -> 'Compiling 184 files (.ex)' / 'Generated letflow app', zero warnings, zero errors.
2. `mix format --check-formatted` -> no output, exit clean (all touched files already formatted).
3. `mix test test/letflow/plugs/admission_test.exs test/letflow/plugs/admission_pipeline_test.exs test/letflow/plugs/` -> 'Result: 111 passed', 0 failures.
4. Spot-checked both mutation-testing claims by reading test/letflow/plugs/admission_test.exs and test/letflow/plugs/admission_pipeline_test.exs directly: the described tests exist, are non-trivial (real DB round trips through Letflow.Router.call/2 for the pipeline-level tests, real Plug.Conn assertions for the plug-level tests), and each independently targets exactly one of the two release mechanisms in a way consistent with ELIXIR-DEV's claimed mutation results. Plausible, not vacuous.

JUDGMENT CALL ON THE DOUBLE-GLOBAL-CONSUMPTION FINDING (the reason for FAIL): this is a real correctness/availability defect, not an acceptable consequence of REQ-216's design, and it should be fixed before merge.

Reasoning: REQ-216's own design doc (lib/letflow/design/req216-admission-control-core.md §0 item 3) defines 'Global cap = pool_size - reserved_headroom' as a budget calibrated to bound the number of CONCURRENT DB-connection-holding operations the system authorizes at once — the entire point of computing it from the actual Repo pool_size. REQ-216's 'composing' rule (a {:tenant, _} acquisition ALSO consumes the global budget) is correct and not in question — it exists so a per-tenant admission still respects the same shared ceiling. The defect is NOT in REQ-216's core semaphore; it is in how REQ-217 wires two SEPARATE top-level acquisitions against that one shared budget for the SAME request, and holds BOTH simultaneously for nearly the request's entire lifetime (the requirement text's own step 4 mandates storing both refs and releasing both only when the response is sent — confirmed in the shipped code: admission.ex's admit/3 stores each successful ref and releases it only via register_before_send/handle_errors at response time, never in between). Concretely: gate 1 acquires a global unit before Plug.Parsers and holds it through the WHOLE request, including all of gate 2's phase. Gate 2, mounted after AuthPipeline, acquires a SECOND global unit (via the tenant call's own composing rule) and holds it through completion too. For the entire span from 'AuthPipeline done' to 'response sent' — the dominant share of a request's wall-clock time, per the requirement text's own citation of REQ-056/ISS-0431's round-trip profiling — one HTTP request holds TWO units of a budget sized to reflect ONE connection's worth of concurrent work, even though the request only ever holds ONE actual DB connection at a time (AuthPipeline's and TenantStatus/dispatch's DB use are sequential within one process, never concurrent). This is confirmed directly in the shipped tests' own comments, not merely theorized: test/letflow/plugs/admission_pipeline_test.exs's AC3 and AC4 tests both state outright that 'global_cap == 2 is the minimum value that admits even ONE full request end to end' — i.e. the effective concurrent-HTTP-request ceiling under this wiring is exactly HALF of pool_size - reserved_headroom, for the ENTIRE remainder of every request past AuthPipeline, not a brief overlap between two instants.

This is not the 'safe, conservative' failure direction REQ-216 itself explicitly praises elsewhere (e.g. its crash-recovery semantics in §5, which are safe because they under-count in a way that only ever WIDENS admission transiently). This is the OPPOSITE direction: a silent, permanent-under-production halving of the documented capacity formula, with no config knob that corrects for it (an operator sizing reserved_headroom or pool_size from REQ-216's own documented formula would get a system that admits half as many concurrent HTTP requests as that formula implies, for a reason nothing in REQ-216's or REQ-217's public design language surfaces as a capacity-planning fact — only in an implementation-level test comment). Under real load this means: needless 503s to legitimate tenants at half the DB pool's actual safe concurrency, defeating a meaningful share of the point of computing global_cap carefully in the first place (REQ-216 §1's whole rationale for atomic composing was to protect the ACTUAL pool from exhaustion — this wiring now protects it at 2x the necessary conservatism, an availability regression relative to intent even though it never causes an unsafe over-admission).

This also is not something ELIXIR-DEV should have caught or fixed unilaterally: the two-separate-gates shape holding both refs for the whole request duration is literally what the requirement text (step-00's context.requirement_text, item 4) and the validated design (lib/letflow/design/req217-http-admission-wiring.md, PASSED twice by CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR at step-01d) specify. step-01d's own checks_performed record shows CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR never analyzed the global-budget arithmetic across the two gates at all — its four verified rework points were the crash-safety trace, the pdict naming convention, the literal-code sweep, and OQ-2's resolution; none of them is 'does this wiring's global-acquisition count per request match REQ-216's calibration intent.' ELIXIR-DEV discovered the effect empirically (a failing test), disclosed it honestly and prominently, and correctly declined to redesign it — that is exactly right, and per this task's own instruction I am doing the same rather than prescribing a fix. A plausible direction for CODE-DESIGNER to evaluate (not mandated here): release the global-only ref once AuthPipeline completes, immediately before the tenant gate's own acquisition, so at most one global unit is ever held per request at a time — closing the gap named in the requirement text ('AuthPipeline's own DB work... covered by the global gate only') without doubling the steady-state cost of the request's dominant remaining phase. Whether that or another shape is right is a design decision, not mine to make.

VERDICT: FAIL, routed to CODE-DESIGNER. All of INV-1 through INV-9 individually PASS or are correctly NOT-APPLICABLE on this diff — the FAIL is solely the double-global-consumption finding above, raised per this task's explicit instruction to render an independent judgment on it. No tenant-isolation, secret-leak, SQL-injection, or unhandled-crash defect was found.
issues: BLOCKER (availability/correctness, not a tenant-isolation or secret-leak defect): a single admitted HTTP request holds TWO units of Letflow.Admission's shared global budget simultaneously for nearly its entire lifetime (from AuthPipeline's completion through response completion), because the global gate's ref is held open across the tenant gate's own composing acquisition rather than released once AuthPipeline's DB work concludes. This halves the effective concurrent-HTTP-request ceiling relative to REQ-216's documented 'pool_size - reserved_headroom' calibration, confirmed directly by test/letflow/plugs/admission_pipeline_test.exs's own AC3/AC4 comments ('global_cap == 2 is the minimum that admits even ONE full request end to end'). Not caught by CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR at step-01d (its four verified rework points did not include this arithmetic). Recommend CODE-DESIGNER evaluate releasing the global-only ref once AuthPipeline completes (immediately before the tenant gate's own acquisition), or another shape that holds at most one global unit per request at a time, then re-run REQ-217's acceptance criteria (in particular AC1/AC3/AC4, which will need re-deriving their minimum-cap arithmetic) before returning to SECURITY-REVIEWER.
